course_description:
In this course students will utilise advanced skills in how to research, locate, interrogate and analyse information, and to practise investigative reporting as journalists. Investigative journalism has power to deliver reporting for the benefit of society via uncovering secrets, holding power to account, correct injustices and demand and interrogate solutions. When done well, it is the kind of reporting that can deliver meaningful change. In this course, students will apply a variety of journalistic research methods - from observation and interviewing to digital and social media investigation, document mining and FOI requests - to deliver a substantial piece of public-interest journalism. Students will make use of technological developments including AI to search and organise information. They will also explore and critique a wide range of industry examples, ensuring their own investigations are inspired and informed by the best industry standards, trends, contexts, and ethical frameworks.

Contemporary investigative reporting is undergoing a profound transformation. This course equips students to develop as journalism practitioners capable of adapting and utlising digital tools, AI and investigative methods amid ongoing exponential technological change and systemic challenges. This course has been designed with industry experts to develop skills to investigate, trace and debunk misinformation online including foreign and home grown disinformation campaigns targeting Australians on social media. Students will produce a portfolio from weekly tasks as they learn to use open-source verification tools, advanced document search, and AI tools for discovery and research which can be applied in their final investigative or feature report.

course_aims: This course aims to provide you with advanced skills and experience in the practice of investigative journalism for the benefit of society.

learning_outcomes.description: Source, construct and disseminate a piece of investigative journalism.
Formulate, compose and assess advanced investigative measures such as Freedom of Information or Right To Information requests.
Critically analyse the diverse needs of audiences in the interests of working towards a more fair, just, inclusive and equitable society.
Embed the traditions, theories, frameworks and codes of ethics in reporting practice with moral courage in decison making.
Apply a wide range of journalistic research methods, including data-driven reporting, social media investigation, interviewing, observation and document-driven reporting.
Critically assess, interpret and apply use of technological developments including AI to search and organise information.

assessment_details.task_description: Throughout the semester, essential practical skills are assigned and submitted in tutorials as a complete portfolio. Students should refer to Blackboard for the portfolio platform. Elements will be released weekly but include: using AI for investigative research and interrogation, digital verification, document discovery, interview and research plans. The portfolio skillset that this portfolio will assess is completed and uploaded in tutorials only so regular attendance and participation is crucial. Your 5 best tasks out of the 8 will form the made. These tasks are designed to support the final assessment task (Major News Investigation). As part of the portfolio students must gain approval (see Blackboard for details) from their tutor in week 9 for their Major News Investigation. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.category: Paper/ Report/ Annotation, Notebook/ Logbook, Portfolio
assessment_details.task_description: This portfolio will require you to submit a substantive piece of investigative journalism. This assessment task requires you to go out and produce a substantive piece of investigative journalism. The portfolio must include four elements: Progress diary/journal and sources list (template provided on Blackboard). A piece of written investigative journalism in either news or feature style. At least one visual or multimedia element, which could include a data visualisation, chart, map, photograph(s), audio, video or another approved visual or multimedia element. The visual elements should enhance and value-add to the investigative story you have produced, and more than one type of visual or multimedia element may be used. AI Coversheet (template provided on Blackboard, this will include ethical and transparency considerations). The investigative story should include a minimum of four primary sources (more is encouraged) and be 800-1000 words. Your tutor needs to approve your investigation by week 9 to manage any possible risks to yourself, or to the public, or to the environment. In instances where the multimedia components of the submission are substantial (e.g. long-form audio or video, photographic essay), a reduction in the word count of the associated story may be approved by your tutor, but this must be negotiated prior to the end of Week 9. Your investigation should be presented digitally, using Shorthand or another approved platform. The text elements of your investigation must also be submitted via TurnItIn, alongside a sources page and research diary/journal (templates available on Blackboard). You will be expected to record your sources and diary as you go so that we can verify the information in your final story. In this course your tutors are prepared to read drafts for the Major News Investigation. However, several conditions apply: Only one draft will be read per student. Drafts for the Major News Investigation assessment must be submitted in class or at a drop-in session in or prior to Week 12. Any drafts received after this time will not be read. Draft reading is embedded in this course to replicate a newsroom environment and as a learning tool to help you develop journalistic writing. Drafts will not be considered over email. Detailed assessment criteria will be provided via Blackboard. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1 Lecture: Introduction to investigative journalism Principles of investigative journalism, the variety of methods and how they have evolved for application in contemporary industry. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 1 Tutorial: Investigative methods Introduction to the Research Matrix. Comparing investigative methods, using different research methods and processes. Attendance in this week is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 2 Lecture: Active Observation and Context Active witnessing, and methods to cover unexpected stories in expected places. This week we explore the important role observation plays in journalism practice and key examples of its use in industry. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 2 Tutorial: Putting observation into action, finding context Observational journalism, and preparing for assessment - how observation methods can be strategically undertaken to deliver the best outcomes. How to conduct rigorous research context for your assessment topic with AI. Attendance in this week is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 3 Lecture: NO LECTURE DUE TO PUBLIC HOLIDAY Selection of readings and guidance to help you develop your assessment: see Blackboard for details
Week 3: NO TUTORIALS DUE TO PUBLIC HOLIDAY Selection of readings and guidance to help you develop your assessment: see Blackboard for details
Week 4 Lecture: Organising Information Tools and methods to organise complex information. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 4 Tutorial: Organising Information Introduction to organising information. Tutorial attendance is critical Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 5 Lecture: Documents, Social Media and Freedom of Informaton requests Social media reporting tools and ethics, adopting a document mindset, and Freedom of Information requests. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 5 Tutorial: Documents, social media and FOI reporting Documents, social media and FOI reporting. Tutorial attendance is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 6 Lecture: Misinformation, Disinformation and Dark Digital Reporting in a post-truth age; how to spot mis-, dis-and mal-information; disinformation agents and entering the deepfake era: perils and opportunities! Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 6 Tutorial: Verification How to tell the difference between fact and fiction - a practical toolset for identifying dis-, mis- and mal-information, and fact-checking or verifying content. Tutorial attendance is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 7 Lecture: Best-practice reporting and journalistic ethics Anonymous sources, vulnerable sources and other ethical issues in public-interest journalism. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 7 Tutorial: Conceptualising an investigation Getting the most from your concept by identifying quality sources (online and in person) ethical approaches and unexpected research angles. Tutorial attendance is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 8 Lecture: Advanced interviewing Advanced interviewing techniques: asking critical questions; structuring an interview; approaching sources; asking difficult questions; trauma-informed interviewing. Attendance in this week is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 8 Tutorial: Developing your investigation Attendance in this week is critical. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 9 Lecture: Storytelling techniques Building a visual narrative: Visual storytelling is critical in investigative pieces. This lecture looks at the role of photojournalism and data visualisations in story production, as well as other multimedia elements. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 9 Tutorial: Developing your investigation Attendance in this week is critical for approval of your investigation topic if not already received. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Mid-Semester Break
Week 10: Masterclass tbc Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 10: NO TUTORIALS Spend this week developing your investigation.
Week 11 Lecture: Non-fiction storytelling techniques Storytelling for impact Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 11 Tutorial: Storytelling workshop Drafting and workshopping your investigations Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 12 Lecture: The Future of Investigative Journalism Looking forward: the role and value of investigative reporting, industry case studies; the future of investigative journalism. Final tips for story submission. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 12 Tutorial: Story workshop This is your final chance to meet your tutor to discuss your assignment. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06
Week 13: NO LECTURE

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
